Connecting Your MCP Client#

In the following, we provide general instructions on how to connect Selene to your MCP-enabled client, as well as specific instructions for popular clients.

General Instructions#

In general, Selene can be used with any MCP-enabled client. To connect Selene to your favourite client, simply

  1. determine how to add a custom MCP server to your client (refer to the client’s documentation).

  2. add a new MCP server entry by specifying either

    • a run command that allows the client to start the MCP server in stdio mode as a subprocess, or

    • the URL of the HTTP/SSE endpoint, having started the Selene MCP server in HTTP/SSE mode beforehand.

Find concrete examples for popular clients below.

Depending on your needs, you might want to further customize Selene’s behaviour by

  • adding command-line arguments

  • adjusting configuration.

Mode of Operation. Note that some clients have a per-workspace MCP configuration (e.g, VSCode and Claude Code), while others have a global MCP configuration (e.g. Codex and Claude Desktop).

  • In the per-workspace case, you typically want to start Selene with your workspace directory as the project directory and never switch to a different project. This is achieved by specifying the --project <path> argument with a single-project context (e.g. ide or claude-code).

  • In the global configuration case, you must first activate the project you want to work on, which you can do by asking the LLM to do so (e.g., “Activate the current dir as project using selene”). In such settings, the activate_project tool is required.

Tool Selection. While you may be able to turn off tools through your client’s interface (e.g., in VSCode or Claude Desktop), we recommend selecting your base tool set through Selene’s configuration, as Selene’s prompts automatically adjust based on which tools are enabled/disabled.
A key mechanism for this is to use the appropriate context when starting Selene.

Common Pitfalls#

Discoverability of the selene command. Your client may not find the selene CLI command, even if it is on your system PATH. In this case, a workaround is to provide the full path to the selene executable.

Selene’s tools not being used. With some clients, you may experience that Selene’s tools are not being used. This is mainly due to problems in the client itself (like a poorly implemented tool discovery). To counteract this, Selene comes with a set of commands that can be used in hooks. See the sections on hooks for Claude Code and VSCode below.

Environment Variables. Some language servers may require additional environment variables to be set (e.g. F# on macOS with Homebrew), which you may need to explicitly add to the MCP server configuration. Note that for some clients (e.g. Claude Desktop), the spawned MCP server process may not inherit environment variables that are only configured in your shell profile (e.g. .bashrc, .zshrc, etc.); they would need to be set system-wide instead. An easy fix is to add them explicitly to the MCP server entry. For example, in Claude Desktop and other clients, you can simply add an env key to the selene object, e.g.

"env": {
    "DOTNET_ROOT": "/opt/homebrew/Cellar/dotnet/9.0.8/libexec"
}

Copilot in JetBrains#

Open the settings of your JetBrains IDE and go to Tools / GitHub Copilot / Model Context Protocol (MCP). Then click on the Configure button. This will open your global mcp.json file, where you can add the following entry for Selene:

{
    "servers": {
      "selene": {
        "type": "stdio",
        "command": "selene",
        "args": [
          "start-mcp-server",
          "--context=jb-copilot-plugin"
        ]
      }
    }
}

Verification. Open Copilot, switch to Agent mode, and click on the configure tools button. You should see Selene’s tools in the list and be able to start the Selene server there (you do not generally have to start Selene in the future, Copilot will start the server by itself). If the server is shown as running, Copilot is successfully connected to Selene. Most models will understand how to use Selene’s tools out of the box, but for some models you may have to prompt “Activate the current project with Selene and read initial instructions” in the beginning of the chat.

Recommended Configuration. The jb-copilot-plugin context (see above) comes with our recommended subset of Selene’s tools for Copilot in JetBrains IDEs. We also recommend disabling the following built-in tools for optimal performance: replace_string_in_file, apply_patch, list_dir, file_search, grep_search. Note that running subagents may not use MCP servers, consider deactivating the run_subagent tool as well.

Selene offers better alternatives to these basic tools. If you do prefer to use the built-in tools instead, you should disable corresponding Selene tools instead to prevent context bloat.

We also recommend marking Selene’s tools as approved so you don’t have to manually approve them in agent sessions. You can do this in Tools / GitHub Copilot / Chat, where at the bottom you can click on the Configure button for MCP tool auto-approval.

Claude Code#

Selene is a great way to make Claude Code both more efficient and more powerful! To set up the Selene MCP server for Claude Code, you can simply run this command:

selene setup claude-code

Find manual setup instructions as well as workarounds for Claude Code’s recent regressions pertaining to (external) tool use below.

Attention

Recent updates to Claude Code (CC) and to the Opus line of models resulted in drastically reduced adherence to instructions pertaining to Selene’s tools.

After extensive analysis, we identified part of the reason to be very long and detailed tool descriptions for built-in tools and parts of the default system prompt. The descriptions of CC’s system tools take almost 16k tokens, cannot be adjusted by the user, and introduce a very strong bias towards internal tools, making it almost impossible to convince Opus 4.7 to use Selene.

As a workaround, we crafted a system prompt that counteracts this bias. When using Selene, we highly recommend that you start CC as

claude --system-prompt="$(selene prompts print-cc-system-prompt-override)"

You can also consider adding the content of selene cc-system-prompt-override to your CLAUDE.md files, but the effect be insufficient for counteracting Claude Code’s bias towards internal tools.

Global Configuration. To add the Selene MCP server for all your projects, use the user-level configuration of claude code and the --project-from-cwd flag:

claude mcp add --scope user selene -- selene start-mcp-server --context claude-code --project-from-cwd

Per-Project Configuration. Alternatively, to add Selene only for the current project in the current directory, use the command:

claude mcp add selene -- selene start-mcp-server --context claude-code --project "$(pwd)"

Verification. Confirm that Claude Code is connected to Selene by running the /mcp command and by reconnecting, if necessary. If Selene fails to start fast enough, you should set MCP_TIMEOUT to a sufficiently high value (e.g. by adding export MCP_TIMEOUT=60000 to your shell profile)

Hooks. Due to recent changes (especially dynamic tool loading) in Claude Code, the agent will often fail to make proper use of Selene’s tools, either by failing to load them in the beginning or by forgetting the instructions in a long session (a behavior known as agent drift). To counteract this, we provide reminder hooks. We strongly recommend setting up the hooks as below (or a variation thereof) for optimal performance of Selene in Claude Code.

Note

While recommended, hooks are an alpha feature. Review failures locally with the user; share diagnostics externally only at their explicit request.

To set up hooks, add the following to your Claude Code settings file (.claude/settings.json in your project directory, or ~/.claude/settings.json globally):

All hooks below are opt-in — include only the ones you want. Add the following to your Claude Code settings file (.claude/settings.json in your project directory, or ~/.claude/settings.json globally):

{
    "hooks": {
        "PreToolUse": [
            {
                "matcher": "",
                "hooks": [
                    {
                        "type": "command",
                        "command": "selene-hooks remind --client=claude-code"
                    }
                ]
            },
            {
                "matcher": "mcp__selene__*",
                "hooks": [
                    {
                        "type": "command",
                        "command": "selene-hooks auto-approve --client=claude-code"
                    }
                ]
            }
        ],
        "SessionStart": [
            {
                "matcher": "",
                "hooks": [
                    {
                        "type": "command",
                        "command": "selene-hooks activate --client=claude-code"
                    }
                ]
            }
        ],
        "SessionEnd": [
            {
                "matcher": "",
                "hooks": [
                    {
                        "type": "command",
                        "command": "selene-hooks cleanup --client=claude-code"
                    }
                ]
            }
        ]
    }
}

The hooks will:

  • remind: Nudge the agent to use Selene’s symbolic tools when it makes too many consecutive grep or read_file calls without using any Selene tools in between.

  • activate: Prompt the agent to activate the project and read Selene’s instructions at session start.

  • cleanup: Clean up hook session data when the session ends.

  • auto-approve: Auto-approve Selene tool calls whenever Claude Code is in a permissive permission mode (acceptEdits or auto), so blanket approvals cover Selene’s destructive tools (e.g. replace_symbol_body, rename_symbol) instead of prompting on every call.

For more details on Claude Code’s hook system, see the Claude Code hooks documentation.

VSCode#

You can add Selene to VSCode by running the MCP: Add Server command. In that dialogue, select the Command (stdio) option. You can decide between installing it globally or in the workspace (only for the currently open project), and the command you should enter depends on that choice. (You will be asked to choose after entering the mcp run command.)

Global. (Recommended) Enter selene start-mcp-server --context=vscode. Unfortunately, due to a bug in VSCode, in this setting Selene won’t be able to activate the project automatically. You will have to remember to prompt “Activate the current dir as project using selene” at the start of each session.

Workspace. Enter selene start-mcp-server --context=vscode --project ${workspaceFolder}. This will allow Selene to automatically activate the project, with the downside that you will have to add Selene to each project you want to use it in.

In both cases, proceed to enter Selene as the name, then select either global or workspace.

Verification. You should be able to see Selene in the tools overview in the AI Chat window.

Hooks. Due to recent changes (especially dynamic tool loading) in VSCode, the agent will often fail to make proper use of Selene’s tools, either by failing to load them in the beginning or by forgetting the instructions in a long session (a behaviour known as agent drift). To counteract this, we provide reminder hooks. We strongly recommend setting up the hooks as below (or a variation thereof) for optimal performance of Selene in VSCode.

The hooks will:

  • remind: Nudge the agent to use Selene’s symbolic tools when it makes too many consecutive grep or read_file calls without using any Selene tools in between.

  • activate: Prompt the agent to activate the project and read Selene’s instructions at session start.

  • cleanup: Clean up hook session data when the session ends.

To set this up, create the file ~/.copilot/hooks/selene-hooks.json with the following content:

{
    "hooks": {
        "PreToolUse": [
            {
                "type": "command",
                "command": "selene-hooks remind --client=vscode"
            }
        ],
        "SessionStart": [
            {
                "type": "command",
                "command": "selene-hooks activate --client=vscode"
            }
        ],
        "Stop": [
            {
                "type": "command",
                "command": "selene-hooks cleanup --client=vscode"
            }
        ]
    }
}

The SessionStart hook also addresses the global configuration limitation mentioned above — it will automatically prompt the agent to activate the project directory, so you no longer need to do this manually.

Copilot CLI#

Use the interactive /mcp add slash command, choose Selene as the name, STDIO as the server type, and selene start-mcp-server --context=copilot-cli --project-from-cwd as command. Copilot CLI will immediately notify you that Selene is running if everything is set up correctly or display an error otherwise.

You should add the same hooks as in VSCode (see above) if Copilot CLI didn’t pick them up automatically.

Codex (CLI and App)#

You can simply run selene setup codex.

Alternatively, you can manually add the following to ~/.codex/config.toml (create the file if it does not exist):

[mcp_servers.selene]
startup_timeout_sec = 15
command = "selene"
args = ["start-mcp-server", "--project-from-cwd", "--context=codex"]

Verification. Run the /mcp command and verify that Selene is connected. The Codex app does not start a session in the project’s directory, so when using the app, we recommend asking Codex to “Activate the current dir as project using selene” at the start of each session (though Codex might do this automatically).

Hooks. Codex supports lifecycle hooks; see the Codex hooks documentation for details. To enable Selene’s hooks for Codex, add this feature flag to ~/.codex/config.toml:

[features]
codex_hooks = true

Then create ~/.codex/hooks.json with the following content:

{
    "hooks": {
        "PreToolUse": [
            {
                "matcher": "Bash",
                "hooks": [
                    {
                        "type": "command",
                        "command": "selene-hooks remind --client=codex"
                    }
                ]
            }
        ],
        "PostToolUse": [
            {
                "matcher": "^mcp__selene__.*$",
                "hooks": [
                    {
                        "type": "command",
                        "command": "selene-hooks reset --client=codex"
                    }
                ]
            }
        ],
        "SessionStart": [
            {
                "matcher": "startup|resume",
                "hooks": [
                    {
                        "type": "command",
                        "command": "selene-hooks activate --client=codex"
                    }
                ]
            }
        ],
        "SessionEnd": [
            {
                "hooks": [
                    {
                        "type": "command",
                        "command": "selene-hooks cleanup --client=codex"
                    }
                ]
            }
        ]
    }
}

The SessionEnd cleanup hook requires Codex 0.145.0 or newer. Older Codex versions only support Stop for cleanup, which currently has a [known compatibility issue](historical issue #1533). If you still configure it, replace SessionEnd with Stop in the example above. Configure cleanup under exactly one of these events, never both: Stop runs after every turn, while SessionEnd runs when Codex tears down the root thread.

The hooks will:

  • activate: Prompt the agent to activate the current project and read Selene’s instructions when a Codex session starts or resumes.

  • remind: Nudge the agent to use Selene’s symbolic tools when it makes too many consecutive code-search or code-file-read calls without using Selene tools in between.

  • reset: Clear the reminder counters after a successful Selene symbolic tool call, so using Selene’s tools starts a fresh count instead of leaving the prior grep/read streak in place.

  • cleanup: Clean up hook session data when the session ends.

The PreToolUse matcher is intentionally restricted to Bash: the reminder hook tracks shell-based grep and code-file reads, so running it for every tool call is unnecessary. That matcher never sees mcp__selene__* tool names, though, so it cannot also perform the counter reset on Selene tool use the way it does for clients whose PreToolUse hook observes every tool call. The separate reset hook above, matched to PostToolUse on Selene’s own tools, covers that case for Codex instead.

Grok#

Selene provides native support for xAI’s Grok Build CLI. To set up the Selene MCP server for Grok, simply run:

selene setup grok

Manual Setup#

Global Configuration. To add the Selene MCP server for all your projects, use Grok’s user-level configuration and the --project-from-cwd flag:

grok mcp add --scope user selene -- selene start-mcp-server --context=grok --project-from-cwd

Alternatively, add the following to ~/.grok/config.toml:

[mcp_servers.selene]
command = "selene"
args = ["start-mcp-server", "--project-from-cwd", "--context=grok"]

Project-Level Configuration. To add the Selene MCP server for a single project only:

grok mcp add --scope project selene -- selene start-mcp-server --context=grok --project "$(pwd)"

Verification. Run grok inspect and verify that Selene is listed as an MCP server. You can also use Grok’s /mcps modal to inspect, refresh, enable, or disable configured MCP servers.

Grok can also load existing Claude Code MCP configuration. If you previously ran selene setup claude-code, Selene may already appear in Grok, but it will use the claude-code context instead of the dedicated grok context.

Hooks#

Grok supports lifecycle hooks; see Grok’s bundled hooks documentation for details. To enable Selene’s hooks for Grok globally, create ~/.grok/hooks/selene-hooks.json with the following content. For a single project, create .grok/hooks/selene-hooks.json in that project instead; note that Grok loads project-scoped hooks only after you have trusted the project for hook execution (via Grok’s /hooks-trust command).

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "grep|read_file|run_terminal_command",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "selene-hooks remind --client=grok",
            "timeout": 5
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "Stop": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "selene-hooks cleanup --client=grok",
            "timeout": 5
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The hooks will:

  • remind: Nudge the agent to use Selene’s symbolic tools when it makes too many consecutive code-search or code-file-read calls without using Selene tools in between.

  • cleanup: Clean up hook session data when the agent turn ends.

Grok ignores stdout from passive hooks such as SessionStart, so the Grok hook setup intentionally uses only PreToolUse for reminders and Stop for cleanup.

Claude Desktop#

On Windows and macOS, there are official Claude Desktop applications by Anthropic; for Linux, there is an open-source community version.

To configure MCP server settings, go to File / Settings / Developer / MCP Servers / Edit Config, which will let you open the JSON file claude_desktop_config.json.

Add the selene MCP server configuration

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "selene": {
      "command": "selene",
      "args": [
        "start-mcp-server",
        "--context=desktop-app"
      ]
    }
  }
}

If your language server requires specific environment variables to be set (e.g. F# on macOS with Homebrew), you can add them via an env key (see above).

Verification. Once you have created the new MCP server entry, save the config and then restart Claude Desktop.

Attention

Be sure to fully quit the Claude Desktop application via File / Exit, as regularly closing the application will just minimize it.

After restarting, you should see Selene’s tools in your chat interface (notice the small hammer icon).

Copilot CLI#

In the interactive mode, you can call /mcp add from within the copilot CLI. There, use selene as name, STDIO as the server type, and selene start-mcp-server --context=copilot-cli --project-from-cwd as command.

Alternatively, add the following to ~/.copilot/mcp-config.json (create the file if it does not exist):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "selene": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "selene",
      "tools": [
        "*"
      ],
      "args": [
        "start-mcp-server",
        "--context=copilot-cli",
        "--project-from-cwd"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Verification. Copilot should now show that Selene is running, though you may have to restart it.

JetBrains Junie#

For the Junie plugin in JetBrains IDEs you can add Selene either to the global configuration in ~/.junie/mcp/mcp.json or to the project configuration in <project>/.junie/mcp/mcp.json. Important, don’t add both! In both cases the entry should be:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "selene": {
      "command": "selene",
      "args": [
        "start-mcp-server",
        "--context=junie",
        "--project-from-cwd"
      ]
    }
  }
}

With the global configuration, Selene will be available in all projects. However, within the Junie plugin, projects will not be automatically activated in Selene. You may thus have to prompt Junie to “Activate the current project using selene’s activation tool” at the start of each session (though some models are smart enough to activate the project automatically).

With the project-scoped configuration, Selene will be available only in that project, and the project will automatically be recognized as active by Selene.

JetBrains AI Assistant#

Go to Settings / Tools / AI Assistant / MCP and enter the following configuration:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "selene": {
      "command": "selene",
      "args": [
        "start-mcp-server",
        "--context=jb-ai-assistant",
        "--project-from-cwd"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Like for Junie, you have the choice between the global and the project-scoped configuration, with the same trade-off.

Antigravity#

Add this configuration:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "selene": {
      "command": "selene",
      "args": [
        "start-mcp-server",
        "--context=antigravity"
      ]
    }
  }
}

You will have to prompt Antigravity’s agent to “Activate the current project using selene’s activation tool” after starting Antigravity in the project directory (once in the first chat enough, all other chat sessions will continue using the same Selene session).

Unlike VSCode, Antigravity does not currently support including the working directory in the MCP configuration. Also, the current client will be shown as none in Selene’s dashboard (Antigravity currently does not fully support the MCP specifications). This is not a problem, all tools will work as expected.

CodeBuddy#

Selene provides native support for CodeBuddy, a CLI coding agent that shares a similar architecture with Claude Code. To set up the Selene MCP server for CodeBuddy, simply run:

selene setup codebuddy

Manual Setup#

Global Configuration. To add the Selene MCP server for all your projects, use the user-level configuration of CodeBuddy and the --project-from-cwd flag:

codebuddy mcp add --scope user selene -- selene start-mcp-server --context codebuddy --project-from-cwd

Project-Level Configuration. To add the Selene MCP server for a single project only:

codebuddy mcp add selene -- selene start-mcp-server --context codebuddy --project "$(pwd)"

Confirm that CodeBuddy is connected to Selene by running the /mcp command and reconnecting if necessary.

Hooks#

CodeBuddy supports the same hook system as Claude Code. To set up hooks, add the following to your CodeBuddy settings file (.codebuddy/settings.json in your project directory, or ~/.codebuddy/settings.json globally):

{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "selene-hooks remind --client=codebuddy"
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "Notification": [
      {
        "matcher": "",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "selene-hooks auto-approve --client=codebuddy"
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "SessionStart": [
      {
        "matcher": "",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "selene-hooks activate --client=codebuddy"
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "Stop": [
      {
        "matcher": "",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "selene-hooks cleanup --client=codebuddy"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Hook Descriptions#

  • remind: Remind the agent to use Selene’s tools instead of built-in grep and read tools.

  • activate: Prompt the agent to activate the project at session start and read Selene’s instructions.

  • cleanup: Clean up hook session data when the session ends.

  • auto-approve: Auto-approve Selene tool calls whenever CodeBuddy is in a permissive permission mode (acceptEdits or auto), so blanket approvals cover Selene’s destructive tools (e.g. replace_symbol_body, rename_symbol) instead of prompting on every call.

Other Clients#

For other clients, follow the general instructions above to set up Selene as an MCP server.

Terminal-Based Clients#

There are many terminal-based coding assistants that support MCP servers, such as

  • Gemini-CLI,

  • Qwen3-Coder,

  • rovodev,

  • OpenHands CLI,

  • opencode and

  • CodeBuddy-Code.

They generally benefit from the symbolic tools provided by Selene. You might want to customize some aspects of Selene by writing your own context, modes or prompts to adjust it to the client’s respective internal capabilities (and your general workflow).

In most cases, the ide context is likely to be appropriate for such clients, i.e. add the arguments --context ide in order to reduce tool duplication.

MCP-Enabled IDEs and Coding Clients (Cline, Roo-Code, Cursor, Windsurf, etc.)#

Most of the popular existing coding assistants (e.g. IDE extensions) and AI-enabled IDEs themselves support connections to MCP Servers. Selene generally boosts performance by providing efficient tools for symbolic operations.

We generally recommend using the ide context for these integrations by adding the arguments --context ide in order to reduce tool duplication.

Local GUIs and Agent Frameworks#

Over the last months, several technologies have emerged that allow you to run a local GUI client and connect it to an MCP server. The respective applications will typically work with Selene out of the box. Some of the leading open source GUI applications are

  • Jan,

  • OpenHands,

  • OpenWebUI and

  • Agno.

These applications allow combining Selene with almost any LLM (including locally running ones) and offer various other integrations.
